prompt: Sort each request by which of the three jobs — draft, edit, or critique — it's actually asking for.

categories.label: Draft
items: “I have five bullet points about the delay — turn this into an email”
“I don't have anything written yet — write me an opening paragraph for a cover letter”

categories.label: Edit
items: “Here's my paragraph — fix the grammar and tighten the second sentence, don't touch the rest”
“Keep my wording, just reorder these two sentences so it flows better”

categories.label: Critique
items: “Don't change anything — just tell me if the tone comes across as annoyed”
“Read this and tell me what a stranger would find confusing, but leave the text as is”

hints: Draft requests start from nothing or from bullet points, not from finished sentences.
Edit requests hand over existing sentences and ask for specific, bounded changes. Critique requests explicitly rule out any rewriting at all.
explanation: Draft requests share one property: there's no finished prose yet, only raw material (bullets, an idea) to be turned into sentences for the first time. Edit requests hand over real sentences and name a specific, bounded change. Critique requests go further than edit requests by explicitly ruling out any rewriting — the text stays untouched and only the assessment of it is wanted.

prompt: You've drafted a short update for your team and want it tightened — not rewritten — before you send it. Write the actual prompt you'd use, naming the method as well as the goal.
hints: Name the boundary explicitly: what may change, and what should stay exactly as you wrote it.
“Tighten” alone is still ambiguous — it could mean cut words or restructure entirely.
explanation: A strong prompt names both the goal and the method: something like “Edit this update — cut anything redundant and tighten wordy sentences, but keep my structure, my wording, and my paragraph order as close to the original as you can. Don't rewrite sentences that are already clear.” The key move is the same as the lesson's worked example — stating the boundary of what may change, not just asking for “better,” which leaves the model to decide how far to go on its own.

prompt: True or false: telling an AI tool “write this in my voice — I'm casual and a little sarcastic” gives it enough to actually produce your specific voice.

config.statement: Telling an AI tool you're “casual and a little sarcastic” gives it enough to produce your specific voice.
config.rubric: A full answer states false and explains that 'casual and sarcastic' describes a broad category shared by many different actual voices, not the writer's specific word choices, sentence habits, or recurring phrases — real samples or named specific habits are needed for that.

hints: How many different people could accurately describe themselves as 'casual and a little sarcastic'?
What's the difference between a category of voice and your specific one?
explanation: False. “Casual and a little sarcastic” is a real description, but it's a category — thousands of distinct voices fit it. It gives the model a register to aim for, not the specific word choices, sentence rhythms, or recurring phrases that make writing recognisably yours. That requires either real samples of your actual writing or specific, nameable habits (“I always undercut a serious point with a one-line joke right after it”), not a personality adjective.

prompt: Name one specific, nameable habit in your own writing — not a vibe word like “casual,” but something concrete an AI tool could actually follow (a sentence-length pattern, a recurring phrase, how you open or close a message, a specific kind of joke or aside). Then write the instruction you'd give to preserve it.
hints: Think of something a close friend would notice if it were missing, not a general adjective about your style.
The instruction should be something the model could check itself against — concrete enough to follow, not just aim toward.
explanation: A strong answer names something concrete: e.g. “I always open work emails with a one-line summary before any explanation”, or “I use short, blunt sentences and almost never use semicolons.” The paired instruction should be equally concrete — e.g. “Open with a one-line summary of the ask before any context. Keep sentences short.” The test for a good answer here isn't the specific habit chosen, it's whether the instruction is something the model could actually check its own output against, rather than another vibe word restated.

prompt: Which of these feedback requests is most likely to produce specific, usable criticism rather than general praise?

options.text: “Acting as a landlord who reads dozens of maintenance-request emails a week, tell me the two things about this email that would make you deprioritize it”
“Is this a good email?”
“How would you rate this email out of 10?”
“What do you think of this?”

hints: Which option names both a specific reader and a specific, bounded thing to find?
The other three all leave the model free to answer with a general, safe impression.
explanation: The landlord version names a specific reader, their actual situation (reading many of these), and a bounded, concrete task (find two things that would deprioritize it) — all three of the levers from this lesson. “Is this good,” a bare numeric rating, and “what do you think” are all open enough to be answered with general praise, which is exactly what tends to happen.

prompt: You ask an AI tool for feedback on a difficult message and get back: “This communicates your point well! You might consider softening the second paragraph slightly.” You suspect it's actually more of a problem than that. Write the follow-up question you'd ask to get past the vague praise.
hints: Recall the exact move from the lesson — what makes a follow-up hard to answer with more empty praise?
Ask for a specific, bounded number of real problems, not a general second opinion.
explanation: A strong follow-up is specific and bounded, e.g.: “If you had to find three real problems with this — not polish suggestions, actual problems — what would they be, and why?” This works because it removes the option of another vague, safe answer: a fixed number of named problems is much harder to fill with compliments than an open-ended “any other thoughts?” would be.

prompt: Match each drafting habit to the specific risk it creates in an emotionally loaded message.

pairs.left: Asking for an “apologetic” message with no real reason supplied
pairs.right: The model fills the gap with a plausible-sounding, possibly false, specific reason

pairs.left: Not stating how much detail to share with a specific reader
pairs.right: The draft either over-discloses or reads as evasively vague, in either case guessing instead of matching your actual boundary

pairs.left: Accepting the first draft's tone without checking against the actual relationship
pairs.right: The register (how apologetic, how formal) may not match what this specific person actually needs to hear from you

right: The message will always come out too long to send as-is
AI drafts of personal messages are legally required to include a disclaimer

hints: Each habit maps to a specific, named risk from the lesson — not a generic 'it might be wrong.'
Both distractors describe things this lesson never claims.
explanation: Each habit creates a distinct, named failure: an unsupplied reason gets a plausible invented one; an unstated disclosure boundary produces either over-sharing or evasive vagueness; and an unchecked tone may not fit the actual relationship, since the model has no way to know how this specific friend or manager reads apologies. Neither distractor reflects anything from the lesson.

prompt: Write the prompt you'd use to draft a message to a coworker letting them know you need to reschedule a call, for a health reason you'd rather not detail. State the disclosure boundary explicitly, the way this lesson describes.
hints: Name exactly what may be said and what shouldn't be, rather than leaving the model to infer an appropriate amount.
You can still ask for a specific tone — just don't leave the amount of medical detail up to the model's guess.
explanation: A strong prompt states both the ask and the exact boundary, e.g.: “Draft a short message to a coworker asking to reschedule our 2pm call. Say only that something health-related came up — don't name a specific condition, appointment, or symptom, and don't apologize excessively. Keep it brief and matter-of-fact.” The specific boundary (“don't name a specific condition”) is what prevents the model from either inventing detail or guessing at how much is appropriate to share with a coworker.

prompt: True or false: any message that involves strong emotion — yours or the recipient's — is one you should write entirely yourself, with no AI involvement at all.

config.statement: Any emotionally loaded message should be written entirely without AI involvement.
config.rubric: A full answer states false and explains that the relevant line is whether part of what the message communicates is that the sender personally did the thinking (grief, real apologies, firsthand references), not emotional intensity generally — structural help is fine even on those, and plenty of emotionally-toned routine messages don't carry that weight at all.

hints: Recall the reschedule-message and status-update examples from the lesson — do those carry the same weight as a condolence note?
The lesson's actual dividing line wasn't 'emotional or not' — what was it?
explanation: False. The lesson's actual line is narrower and more specific: whether part of what a message communicates is that the sender personally did the thinking — which is true of condolence notes, real apologies, and firsthand references, but not of every emotionally-toned message (an anxious but routine reschedule request doesn't carry that weight). And even within the category that does carry it, structural help — checking length or whether a line lands wrong — remains fine, as long as the actual sentiment stays the sender's own.

prompt: Think of a real piece of writing from your own life that belongs on the “write it yourself” list from this lesson. Write the structural-help-only prompt you'd use for it — one that gets feedback on execution without asking the model to generate the sentiment.
hints: The prompt should include your own actual words already written, and ask only about length, clarity, or tone — not ask it to write or rewrite the sentiment.
A good test: could you delete the AI's answer entirely and the message would still say something true about who did the thinking?
explanation: A strong answer names a real personal category (a condolence note, an apology, a reference) and a prompt structured like: “Here's what I've written [pasted in]. Don't rewrite anything or add sentiment I didn't include — just tell me if the length feels right for the situation and whether any sentence reads as more about me than about them.” The key test is whether the prompt asks for anything beyond execution feedback — any request to generate or substantially rework the sentiment itself fails the point of this lesson, even if it produces a technically better-written message.

prompt: You've written a paragraph and want only the second sentence tightened, nothing else touched. Which prompt actually gets you that?

options.text: “Edit this — tighten only the second sentence. Leave every other sentence exactly as written.”
“Make this better.”
“Rewrite this to be more concise.”
“Improve the flow of this paragraph.”

hints: Which option names both the exact scope (one sentence) and the boundary (nothing else changes)?
The other three all leave the model free to rewrite the whole paragraph.
explanation: Only the first option names a bounded edit — which sentence, and an explicit instruction to leave the rest untouched. “Make this better,” “rewrite to be concise,” and “improve the flow” are all goal-only instructions of the exact kind lesson 1 warns about — each leaves the model free to rewrite more than intended.

prompt: True or false: pasting three examples of your past writing into a prompt guarantees the AI draft will preserve every one of your specific quirks.

config.statement: Pasting past writing samples guarantees every specific quirk gets preserved in the new draft.
config.rubric: A full answer states false and explains that samples help a lot but fluency-optimized drafting still tends to smooth idiosyncratic quirks like interrupting asides unless those are also named explicitly, and a final pass checking for what got sanded off is still worth doing.

hints: Recall the newsletter writer's cat joke, even after real samples were supplied.
Samples help enormously — the question is whether they're sufficient on their own.
explanation: False. Real samples are the right foundation — far better than a vibe description — but lesson 2's own example showed a specific, repeated quirk (a mid-sentence aside) still get smoothed out even with samples supplied, because fluency-optimized drafting treats interruptions as noise by default. Naming the specific quirk to keep, and doing a final pass checking for what got flattened, are both still worth doing.

prompt: A friend asks an AI tool “how's this sound?” about a toast she's writing for a wedding, and gets “This is heartfelt and well-written! Maybe add one more specific memory.” She wants sharper notes. Write the follow-up question that would actually get them.
hints: Name a specific reader or situation, and explicitly rule out more praise.
A fixed, small number of specific weak points is harder to fill with compliments than an open question.
explanation: A strong follow-up: “Skip anything positive — tell me the two moments in this toast that would make people's attention drift, and why.” This names a bounded, specific ask (two moments) and removes the option to answer with more general praise, which is exactly what the vague “how's this sound” invited the first time.

prompt: Sort each message by whether it belongs on the “write it yourself” list from this module, or is fine to fully draft with AI.

categories.label: Write it yourself
items: A message telling a close friend you're sorry for something you said that hurt them
A eulogy for a family member

categories.label: Fine to draft with AI
items: A reminder email about an upcoming meeting
A request to a vendor to resend an invoice

hints: The line isn't 'is this emotional' — it's whether part of the point is proving you personally did the thinking.
Routine and logistical messages, even slightly awkward ones, don't carry that weight.
explanation: A real apology and a eulogy both implicitly claim the sender personally reckoned with what's being said — outsourcing the sentiment changes what's actually true about the message, even if the words read fine. A meeting reminder and an invoice request are purely logistical — nothing about them claims personal emotional effort, so drafting help costs nothing there.

prompt: Put these four steps of turning a vague writing request into a specific one in the order this module's lessons build them.

items: Decide which of the three jobs you actually want: draft, edit, or critique
If it's an edit, name the exact boundary of what may change
If you want feedback, name a specific reader or failure mode instead of asking 'what do you think'
Check any specific factual detail in the result against what's actually true

hints: This follows the module's own build order: name the job first, then bound it, then sharpen it, then verify it.
You can't name a boundary for an edit before you've decided editing is actually the job you want.
explanation: Naming the job first (lesson 1) is the foundation everything else depends on. Bounding an edit and sharpening a feedback request (lessons 1 and 3) both refine a specific one of those jobs. Checking specific factual detail (lesson 4) applies regardless of which job it was, and matters most on the messages where an invented detail would actually cost something.

prompt: You need to tell a coworker you're stepping away for a medical reason without going into detail. Which prompt best matches this module's guidance on disclosure?

options.text: “Draft a short message saying only that something health-related came up — don't name a condition or symptom, don't over-apologize”
“Draft a message explaining exactly what's medically going on so they understand”
“Draft a message and let it decide how much detail feels appropriate”
“Draft the most apologetic version possible, to be safe”

hints: Which option states the exact disclosure boundary rather than leaving it to the model's guess?
Over-explaining and letting the model guess are both the failure modes this module warns about.
explanation: The correct option states the disclosure boundary explicitly — exactly the move from lesson 4's second pod. Explaining the full medical situation oversells detail nobody asked for; letting the model “decide” re-introduces the guessing problem the lesson warns against; and maximizing apology doesn't address disclosure at all, it just risks an over-apologetic register that may not match the situation.

prompt: Pick one real piece of your own writing from the last month — an email, a message, a post. Name which of the three jobs (draft, edit, critique) it actually needed, and whether you asked for that job specifically or let a vague request decide it for you.
hints: Be honest about the mismatch if there was one — that's the useful part of the answer, not an idealized version.
If you didn't use AI on it at all, pick a piece where you would have, and reason through which job it would have needed.
explanation: A strong answer names something real and specific (e.g. 'a message to my landlord about a repair'), correctly identifies which job it needed (often edit, since most real writing starts from something already drafted by hand), and honestly names whether the actual request specified that or left it open. The value of the exercise is in the honest self-check, not in having gotten it right the first time — noticing 'I always just say make this better' is itself a useful, actionable finding.

prompt: You want to know what a specific 12-page insurance policy actually says about pre-authorization. Which approach is structurally safer?

options.text: Upload or paste the actual policy document and ask it to summarise the pre-authorization section specifically
Ask “what do pre-authorization requirements usually look like for a plan like this?”
Ask the AI tool to guess based on the insurer's name alone
Both approaches are equally reliable, since both produce a confident answer

hints: Which option gives the model your actual document to read, rather than a general category to reconstruct from memory?
Confidence in tone isn't evidence of which mode produced the answer.
explanation: Providing the actual document grounds the summary in the real text, which is checkable. “Usually look like” and guessing from the insurer's name alone both pull from a blended, generic memory that may not reflect this specific policy's actual terms — and both can sound exactly as confident as a grounded answer, which is the trap.

prompt: You pasted in a 15-page lease and the AI summary states: “The lease requires 60 days' written notice before moving out.” This matters — you're deciding when to send your notice. What exactly would you do before relying on that number?
hints: What's the specific follow-up request that turns a summarised claim into a checkable one?
You already have the actual document — use that.
explanation: The right move is to ask the model to quote the exact sentence in the lease stating the notice period, then read that quoted sentence yourself against the actual document (or search the document directly for '60 days' or 'notice'). Either the quote is really there and matches, in which case the number is grounded, or it isn't — in which case you've caught an error before it affected a real decision. Trusting the summarised number without locating it in the source text repeats the exact risk this lesson names.

prompt: True or false: asking for “an accurate, concise summary” is enough, on its own, to reliably preserve the caveats and limitations stated in a source document.

config.statement: Asking for 'an accurate, concise summary' reliably preserves caveats and limitations.
config.rubric: A full answer states false and explains that 'accurate' doesn't specify accurate about the caveats specifically, and 'concise' actively pushes toward cutting exactly the qualifying detail that makes a summary longer — an explicit instruction naming caveats/limitations is needed.

hints: Can a summary be 'accurate' about the core finding while still dropping the caveat attached to it?
What does 'concise' reward cutting first?
explanation: False. 'Accurate' says nothing about being accurate specifically regarding limitations — a summary can correctly state the core finding while dropping the caveat and still read as accurate on its own narrow terms. 'Concise' actively works against caveat preservation, since hedges are exactly the kind of qualifying detail that makes a sentence longer. Preserving caveats requires naming them explicitly as something to keep, even at a length cost.

prompt: You're about to rely on an AI summary of your employer's remote-work policy to plan next month. Write the specific follow-up question you'd ask to check for a dropped exception clause, the way the annual-enrollment example in this lesson illustrates.
hints: The question should ask specifically about conditions or exceptions, not just 'is this accurate?'
Tie the question to your actual situation (timing, your specific circumstances) if relevant.
explanation: A strong follow-up is specific and targeted, e.g.: “Are there any exceptions, conditions, or time periods mentioned in the policy where this rule doesn't apply, or applies differently?” This works because it names the exact thing this lesson shows gets dropped — a conditional exception — rather than a general request to double-check, which doesn't reliably surface it.

prompt: Two product manuals give different maintenance intervals for the same part. Which prompt is most likely to surface that conflict rather than smooth over it?

options.text: “Where do these two manuals disagree? Quote the exact relevant sentence from each.”
“Compare these two manuals.”
“What's the overall maintenance schedule for this part?”
“Summarise the consensus across both manuals.”

hints: Which option explicitly asks for disagreement and requires quoting each source separately?
The other three all name a goal that a smoothed, blended answer can technically satisfy.
explanation: Only the first option explicitly asks for disagreement and requires quoting each source individually, which forces the two figures to sit side by side rather than getting merged into one narrative. 'Compare,' 'overall schedule,' and 'consensus' are all goals a flattened, agreement-reading answer can satisfy without ever naming the actual conflict.

prompt: You've gathered four sources on whether a specific supplement interacts with a common medication: a pharmacist's published guidance, a peer-reviewed study, a supplement manufacturer's website, and a forum thread. Write the prompt you'd use to compare them in a way that respects how differently reliable they are.
hints: Name what kind of source each one is, not just its content.
Ask for attribution and for disagreement to be flagged, not for one blended answer.
explanation: A strong prompt asks for both attribution and quality context, e.g.: “Compare what each of these four sources says about this interaction. For each claim, note which source it's from and what kind of source it is (pharmacist guidance, peer-reviewed study, manufacturer site, forum post). Flag anywhere they disagree — don't average them into one answer.” This keeps the manufacturer's and forum's much lower reliability visible instead of letting them contribute equally to a blended 'overall picture,' and it surfaces disagreement instead of resolving it on the reader's behalf.

prompt: True or false: because a search-connected AI tool can retrieve information published after its training cutoff, a confidently cited source from it can be trusted without checking who published it or when.

config.statement: A confidently cited source from a search-connected tool can be trusted without checking who published it or when.
config.rubric: A full answer states false and explains that search-connectivity fixes staleness (access to recent information) but not source-quality judgment — a real, findable, cited source can still be low-quality, unofficial, or misdated, and needs the same independent check as any other claim.

hints: Recall the forum thread re-indexed to look recent — was the citation itself fake, or just misleading about quality and date?
What specifically does search access solve, and what does it leave to the reader?
explanation: False. Search-connectivity solves the recency problem — the tool can find things published after training ended — but it doesn't solve the judgment problem of whether a found source is actually authoritative or actually current. A citation can be entirely real (a genuine, findable page) while still being a poor source: unofficial, outdated despite a recent 'last modified' date, or simply wrong. The citation existing is not the same as the citation being good.

prompt: A search-connected AI tool gives you a specific, current-sounding number for a tax deadline and cites a source. You have three minutes before you need to act on it. What exactly do you check in those three minutes?
hints: You don't have time to fully research the topic — what's the one highest-value check?
Where would the actual authoritative version of a tax deadline live?
explanation: The highest-value three-minute check: click through to the actual cited source and look at two things — is it the tax authority's own official page (or a page directly quoting/linking one), and does the date on it genuinely reflect this year's current rule rather than an old page that's merely been reshared or re-indexed recently. If the citation isn't the authority's own page, a fast second check is searching the tax authority's site directly for the same figure, since that's the one source type this specific claim actually needs to trace back to.

prompt: An AI summary of a long clinical trial protocol states a specific dosage that a decision about your own treatment plan depends on. What's the single best next step?

options.text: Ask where in the protocol document that dosage figure appears, then read that exact section yourself
Read the entire protocol document from the beginning
Trust the figure, since it was stated with a specific, precise number
Ask a different AI tool to restate the same summary

hints: Which option targets the exact claim the decision depends on, without requiring a full re-read?
Precision in a number isn't evidence it's accurate — this was covered earlier in this track.
explanation: Locating and reading the exact section the dosage figure comes from directly checks the one claim that matters, without the time cost of reading the entire document. Reading it all is thorough but usually unnecessary and often impractical; trusting a precise-sounding number is exactly the precision trap from earlier in this track; and asking a different AI tool to restate the same summary doesn't check it against the actual source at all.

prompt: Describe a real, long document you've had (or could imagine having) summarised for you — a policy, a report, a set of instructions. Name the one claim in a hypothetical summary of it that would actually be worth a targeted check, and explain why that one and not the others.
hints: The right answer names the claim the decision actually turns on, not just the most surprising or memorable-sounding one.
A claim you'd act on immediately is a stronger candidate than one that's just background context.
explanation: A strong answer names a real document (e.g. a landlord's move-out policy, a workplace benefits guide, a prescription insert) and identifies the specific claim that would actually change a real decision if wrong — for example, a deadline, a dollar figure, or a dosage — rather than a background detail that's interesting but not decision-critical. The reasoning should explicitly connect back to 'this is the part the decision depends on,' not just 'this seems important.'

prompt: You want to know what your specific employment contract says about non-compete terms. Which is the safer request?

options.text: Paste in the actual contract and ask it to summarise the non-compete section
Ask “what do non-compete clauses usually say?”
Ask it to guess based on your job title and industry
Ask it to compare your situation to a typical case, without providing the contract

hints: Which option grounds the answer in your actual document rather than a generic pattern?
explanation: Only pasting the actual contract grounds the summary in your real, specific terms. 'Usually say,' guessing from job title, and comparing to a 'typical case' all pull from a blended memory that may not reflect your actual contract's specific language at all.

prompt: An AI summary of a clinical guideline says “this treatment is recommended.” The actual guideline says “recommended for patients under 65 without other risk factors; evidence in older patients is limited.” What went wrong, and what would you ask for to prevent it?
hints: This is the caveat-dropping pattern from lesson 2 — name it specifically.
What instruction would have kept the age and risk-factor qualifiers in?
explanation: The summary dropped the guideline's stated conditions (age under 65, no other risk factors) and the caveat about limited evidence elsewhere, converting a conditional recommendation into an unconditional one — exactly the caveat-dropping pattern from this module. Asking explicitly for “any conditions, limitations, or caveats attached to this recommendation, even if it makes the summary longer” is the fix that targets this specifically.

prompt: True or false: if two sources genuinely disagree, the most useful AI comparison is the one that resolves the disagreement into a single clear answer.

config.statement: The most useful comparison of two disagreeing sources resolves the disagreement into a single clear answer.
config.rubric: A full answer states false and explains that resolving a genuine disagreement into one answer (without the authority to know which source is right) hides the conflict the reader actually needs to see and decide about — the useful comparison names and quotes the disagreement instead.

hints: Recall the two insurance policies with opposite coverage decisions — what did the reader actually need to know?
Who is actually positioned to decide which source applies to a specific real situation?
explanation: False. When sources genuinely disagree, resolving that into a single tidy answer hides the actual finding — that a real decision needs to be made about which source applies. The model usually has no way to know which source is correct for a specific person's situation; the useful comparison names the disagreement and quotes each source, so the reader (who does have that context) can decide, rather than having the conflict quietly smoothed away.

prompt: Sort each situation by whether search-connectivity actually helps with it, or leaves the underlying risk unaddressed.

categories.label: Search-connectivity helps
items: Finding out whether a policy changed after the model's training cutoff
Locating whether a specific recent event happened at all

categories.label: Search-connectivity doesn't fix this
items: Judging whether a cited source is actually authoritative
Telling a genuine original-publish date from a recent reshare date

hints: Search fixes one specific problem: access to information published after training ended.
Quality and date judgment about what gets found are separate problems search access doesn't solve on its own.
explanation: Search-connectivity directly solves the staleness problem — finding out something changed, or that a recent event occurred, requires access to information the model wasn't trained on, which search provides. It does not solve judging whether a found source is actually authoritative, or distinguishing a genuine original date from a reshare date — both still require the reader to check the source itself.

prompt: Put these four steps of handling a long document you need summarised in the order this module builds them.

items: Provide the actual document rather than asking from memory, if it exists and you have access to it
Explicitly ask for any caveats, exceptions, or limitations to be included
If comparing to other sources, ask where they disagree rather than for a blended overall picture
Identify the one or two decision-critical claims and locate exactly where in the source they come from

hints: This follows the module's build order: ground it, keep its caveats, compare it honestly, then verify the part that matters.
You can't meaningfully ask 'where do these disagree' before you've established grounded, caveat-preserving summaries of each one individually.
explanation: Grounding the summary in the real document (lesson 1) is the foundation. Preserving caveats (lesson 2) keeps that grounded summary honest about its own limits. Comparing multiple sources honestly (lesson 3) builds on having reliable individual summaries to compare. Targeted verification of the decision-critical claim (lesson 5) is the final check applied to whatever summary — single-source or compared — you're actually about to act on.

prompt: A search-connected tool cites a page for a claim about current guidance. The page's 'last updated' date is this month. What does that date actually tell you?

options.text: Only that the page was modified or republished this month — not necessarily that its actual content or the guidance itself is current
That the guidance described is definitely current, since the page was recently updated
Nothing at all — 'last updated' dates are never meaningful
That the AI tool verified the content's accuracy as of that date

hints: Recall the syndicated, republished article from this module's fourth lesson.
A modification date and a content-currency claim are two different things.
explanation: A 'last updated' date only tells you when the page itself was touched — which can mean a genuine content update, or just a reshare, syndication, or template change with the underlying content untouched. It doesn't mean the AI tool verified anything, and it doesn't guarantee the actual guidance described is current — that still requires checking the source itself, per this module's fourth lesson.

prompt: Think of a real long document in your own life you've either had summarised by AI or would want to. Name: whether you provided the actual document or asked from memory, whether you checked for caveats, and what the one decision-critical claim would be worth verifying directly.
hints: Be honest about which of these steps you actually did versus skipped.
If you haven't done this yet, reason through what you'd do differently after this module.
explanation: A strong answer names something real and specific (a lease, a benefits handbook, a research article relevant to a health decision), honestly assesses whether the document was actually provided versus asked from memory, whether caveats were checked, and correctly identifies the single claim that would matter most to verify directly — not the most interesting detail, but the one an actual decision depends on. The value here is the honest self-audit, matching the practice-set framing from the writing module.

prompt: You've used basic spreadsheet formulas (SUM, IF) but never a lookup function, and want VLOOKUP explained. Which request is most likely to land at the right level?

options.text: “I know basic formulas like SUM and IF but have never used a lookup function — explain VLOOKUP starting from there”
“Explain VLOOKUP simply”
“Explain VLOOKUP like I'm 5”
“What is VLOOKUP?”

hints: Which option actually states existing knowledge rather than a vague target level?
The other three all leave the model to guess a default level with no anchor.
explanation: Only the first option gives the model an actual anchor — what you already know — to calibrate the explanation against. “Simply,” “like I'm 5,” and the bare question all leave the level entirely to the model's default guess, which may land too basic (re-explaining formulas you already know) or too advanced (assuming lookup-function familiarity you don't have).

prompt: You want to understand a term your doctor used, without sounding like you're spiraling and without getting a flattened, unhelpful oversimplification. Write the actual prompt you'd use.
hints: State your actual background explicitly rather than letting your phrasing signal it by accident.
Include a request to check afterward whether the depth actually landed.
explanation: A strong prompt states background directly and asks for a real explanation, not a gloss: “My doctor mentioned [term] and I want to actually understand what it means and why it's relevant to me — I don't have a medical background, but I don't want the simplest possible version either. After you explain it, ask me if it makes sense or if you should adjust.” Naming both 'no medical background' and 'don't oversimplify' heads off both failure directions from the lesson at once.

prompt: True or false: if an explanation makes complete sense while you're reading it, that's reliable evidence you'll be able to explain or use it later without the text in front of you.

config.statement: An explanation making complete sense while reading it reliably predicts you'll be able to use it later without the text.
config.rubric: A full answer states false and explains that reading tests recognition (does this make sense as I go), not recall (can I generate this myself), and the two are different skills — feeling like it made sense doesn't test the retrieval pathway that using it later requires.

hints: Recall the coworker who blanked despite feeling like it 'clicked' while reading.
What's actually being tested while you read fluently — recognizing correct information, or producing it yourself?
explanation: False. Reading tests whether you can recognise correct information as it's presented — a genuinely easier task than generating that same information yourself from memory later. Feeling like something 'made sense' while reading is real, but it's evidence about recognition, not recall, and recall is the skill that explaining or applying the concept later actually depends on.

prompt: You just read an AI explanation of a new concept for work and want to actually test whether it stuck. Write the quizzing prompt you'd use, applying the specific techniques from this lesson.
hints: Avoid multiple choice — ask for something that forces you to generate an answer with nothing to recognise it against.
Consider asking for a scenario or an explain-it-back format, with feedback withheld until you've answered.
explanation: A strong prompt asks for genuine generation, e.g.: “Don't give me multiple choice. Give me a realistic scenario where I'd need to use this, ask me what I'd do and why, and don't tell me if I'm right until after I've answered.” Or: “Ask me to explain this back to you in my own words first, then tell me what I got right, missed, or got wrong.” Either version removes the recognition shortcut that a list of options or immediate feedback would provide.

prompt: Why can a well-organized, clearly worded AI explanation feel like genuine understanding even when it hasn't produced any?

options.text: The felt ease of following a smooth explanation and the felt ease of actually understanding something feel similar from the inside, so one gets mistaken for the other
AI explanations are never actually clear, so this only happens with poorly written ones
It only happens to people who aren't paying close attention while reading
It doesn't happen — a clear explanation always produces real understanding

hints: The mechanism is about two similar-feeling but different things being confused, not about attention or explanation quality.
One is about how the text was written; the other is about what ends up in your head.
explanation: The fluency illusion happens precisely because clarity and comprehension produce a similar felt sense of ease — the smoother and more well-organized the explanation, the more likely that similarity is to fool you, regardless of how carefully you were reading. It's not a failure of attention, and it doesn't require a badly written explanation — if anything, the clearer the explanation, the stronger the illusion.

prompt: Think of something you learned recently from an AI explanation that felt completely clear at the time. Describe the specific unaided test you'd run now to check whether real understanding actually stuck, and be honest about what you predict the result would be.
hints: Pick a real, specific thing you learned, not a hypothetical.
The test should remove the source — explain it unaided, apply it to something new, or recall it after time has passed.
explanation: A strong answer names something specific and real (e.g. 'how a particular tax deduction works,' or 'the mechanism behind a medication interaction I looked up'), describes a genuine unaided test (closing the source and explaining it from scratch, or applying it to a new example), and gives an honest prediction rather than an assumed pass — the value of the exercise is in actually running the test mentally and noticing where the explanation, not the understanding, is what's left.

prompt: True or false: an expert reading a subtly wrong AI explanation and a true beginner reading the exact same explanation are equally likely to notice something's off.

config.statement: An expert and a true beginner are equally likely to notice a subtly wrong explanation.
config.rubric: A full answer states false and explains that noticing an inconsistency requires already knowing enough about the topic to compare the explanation against — which is exactly what a true beginner lacks, making them structurally less able to catch the error than someone with existing knowledge.

hints: What does noticing 'something's off' actually require you to already have?
Recall the student who built on a wrong concept for weeks without noticing.
explanation: False. Noticing an inconsistency requires having something to compare the new explanation against — prior knowledge an expert has and a true beginner, by definition, doesn't. This is exactly why beginners are structurally worse positioned to catch a subtly wrong explanation, and why the compounding risk this lesson describes falls hardest on exactly the learners least equipped to catch it early.

prompt: You're learning a new-to-you concept from AI explanations over several sessions and plan to use it to make a real decision soon. Describe specifically when, in that process, you'd stop and cross-check against a second source — not 'always' or 'never,' but the specific point this lesson's heuristic points to.
hints: Use the proportional heuristic: newness, how foundational it is, and how consequential being wrong would be.
The right moment is usually right before you build on it or pass it to someone else, not at the very first explanation.
explanation: A strong answer identifies the point where the concept is about to be relied on — right before it's used to make the actual decision, or right before teaching it to someone else — rather than checking every single explanation as it comes in, or never checking at all. The reasoning should explicitly invoke the three factors from the lesson: how new the concept still is, how foundational it is to what comes next, and how consequential a wrong version would be if acted on.

prompt: On a low-energy day, why might passive AI-explained reading feel like productive studying while actually building little retained understanding?

options.text: It produces the same fluency illusion as any easy-to-follow explanation, while requiring almost no genuine cognitive engagement to get through
AI explanations are less accurate on low-energy days
Passive reading is always worthless, regardless of energy level
It only feels unproductive in hindsight, with no real mechanism behind it

hints: Connect this back to the fluency illusion from earlier in the module.
The issue isn't accuracy — it's what the reading experience actually builds.
explanation: This is the fluency illusion from earlier in the module, showing up specifically on a low-energy day: an easy, passive read feels like progress because it was easy to follow, not because it built retained understanding — and that gap is easy to miss precisely on a day when checking for it also feels like too much effort.

prompt: Describe a low-energy study cycle you could actually use on a foggy day, for something you're currently trying to learn — naming the one concept, what you'd attempt before the explanation, and the unaided check at the end.
hints: Keep the scope to exactly one concept — that's what makes real engagement affordable.
The end check should require nothing in front of you, not just a feeling of clarity.
explanation: A strong answer names one specific, narrow concept (not a whole topic), a genuine attempt before looking at the explanation (even a guess), and an unaided check at the end that requires actually producing something — saying it back in one sentence with nothing to read from — rather than just noting that the explanation felt clear, which this module has already shown isn't reliable evidence of anything.

prompt: You already understand basic statistics (mean, median, standard deviation) and want to learn about p-values. Which request calibrates best?

options.text: “I understand mean, median, and standard deviation — explain p-values building from that, not from scratch”
“Explain p-values simply”
“Explain p-values like I've never seen statistics before”
“What are p-values?”

hints: Which option states existing knowledge as an actual anchor?
explanation: Naming existing knowledge directly gives the model an actual starting point to build from — the other three all leave the level to a default guess, risking either a re-explanation of concepts already known or an assumption of familiarity that isn't there.

prompt: True or false: a multiple-choice quiz generated by an AI tool tests recall roughly as well as being asked to explain the concept from a blank page.

config.statement: A multiple-choice quiz tests recall about as well as explaining a concept from a blank page.
config.rubric: A full answer states false and explains that multiple choice remains largely a recognition task (picking the right answer from options present), while explaining from a blank page forces genuine generation with nothing to recognise against.

hints: What's actually different about having options in front of you versus having none?
explanation: False. Multiple choice still gives you the correct answer to recognise among the options, which is a substantially easier task than generating the answer with nothing in front of you. Explaining from a blank page or answering an open scenario question forces genuine recall in a way multiple choice mostly doesn't.

prompt: You just finished reading a very clear AI explanation of how compound interest works and it felt completely obvious. Describe the specific unaided test that would tell you whether that's real understanding or the fluency illusion.
hints: The test needs to remove the source and require you to produce something, not just recognise it.
explanation: A strong test removes the explanation entirely and asks for generation: close the source and explain compound interest in your own words, or work through a new example (a different principal, rate, and time period) without looking anything up, then check your own answer. If either of those is noticeably harder than the reading felt, that gap is the actual signal — the fluency of the original explanation, not evidence of what's retained.

prompt: Sort each situation by whether cross-checking a foundational AI explanation against a second source is clearly worth the extra time, or not really necessary here.

categories.label: Worth cross-checking
items: A core concept you're about to teach to a colleague as settled fact
A foundational idea you'll be building the rest of a course's material on top of

categories.label: Not really necessary here
items: A minor, self-contained detail with no bearing on anything else you're learning
A concept you already have independent, solid prior knowledge of

hints: Use the proportional heuristic: newness, how foundational it is, and how consequential being wrong would be.
Something self-contained or already independently known doesn't carry the same compounding risk.
explanation: Concepts about to be taught forward or built upon carry real compounding risk if wrong, which is exactly where a second-source check is proportionate. A self-contained, low-consequence detail, or something you already have solid independent knowledge of, doesn't carry that same risk — cross-checking there is diminishing-returns effort, not the module's actual guidance.

prompt: Put these four moves in the order this module builds them, from getting an explanation to being confident it actually stuck.

items: State what you already know so the explanation is pitched at the right level
Attempt an answer yourself before or instead of just reading the explanation
If it's foundational, cross-check it against a second source before relying on it
Test with the source removed — explain it unaided or apply it to something new

hints: This follows the module's build order: calibrate, engage actively, verify the foundation, then confirm retention.
explanation: Calibrating the level (lesson 1) makes the explanation itself useful. Attempting recall actively (lesson 2) builds a stronger version of the knowledge than passive reading. Cross-checking foundational concepts (lesson 4) catches an error before it compounds. Testing with the source removed (lesson 3) is the final honest check on whether any of it actually stuck.

prompt: On a genuinely low-energy day, which is the better use of limited capacity for learning something new, per this module?

options.text: One narrow concept, with a quick attempt at the answer before reading the explanation, and a one-sentence unaided check after
As much passive reading as you can manage, since active recall takes too much energy on a bad day
A full normal-length session, just read more slowly
Skipping the explanation and going straight to a multiple-choice quiz

hints: Recall the low-energy study cycle from lesson 5 — what made it work despite being short?
explanation: A narrowed, single-concept cycle with a retrieval attempt before the explanation and an unaided check after is short enough to fit low capacity while still forcing real engagement — which is what makes it worth the energy spent, unlike passive reading, which costs real capacity but tends to build little retained understanding.

prompt: Think of something you're currently trying to learn with AI help. Name your actual current habit for each of: level-calibration, quizzing yourself, and checking foundational concepts — and be honest about which of the three you're actually skipping.
hints: Be specific and honest about the real habit, not the ideal one.
Naming which one you skip and why is more useful here than claiming to do all three well.
explanation: A strong answer names a real, current learning effort and honestly assesses each of the three habits — most people are doing at least one by accident (e.g. stating background naturally) and skipping at least one (most commonly the unaided retrieval check, since it's the one that requires the most deliberate extra effort). The honest self-audit is the point, matching the practice-set framing used in earlier modules of this phase.

prompt: True or false: because an appeal letter is a formal, consequential document, using AI to draft it is riskier than just not having the energy to write one and letting the deadline pass.

config.statement: Using AI to draft an appeal letter is riskier than letting the deadline pass due to lack of energy.
config.rubric: A full answer states false and explains that a checked, fact-verified AI draft is a legitimate accommodation for genuinely limited capacity, and the real risk to manage is unverified specific facts in the draft — not the act of using AI assistance itself, which is far lower-cost than a missed deadline.

hints: What actually happens if the deadline passes with nothing written at all?
The real risk this lesson names isn't 'using AI' — what specifically is it?
explanation: False. A missed appeal deadline is a real, often irreversible cost. A drafted-and-verified letter, where every specific fact is checked against actual records before submission, carries a manageable, well-defined risk — not the drafting process itself, but unverified specifics inside it. Framing AI assistance as inherently riskier than not writing the letter at all ignores which of the two outcomes is actually worse.

prompt: You need to appeal a denied accommodation request at work. Describe exactly what you'd provide to the AI tool before asking for a draft, and what you'd check before sending it — applying this lesson's two-part approach.
hints: Name the actual documents to paste in, not just a description of the situation.
Name the specific kinds of claims worth checking — dates, references, prior conversations — not a general 'read it carefully.'
explanation: A strong answer names concrete inputs: the actual denial email or letter, any relevant policy text, and notes on prior conversations about the request, provided in full rather than summarized from memory. Before sending, it names specific things to check — any date mentioned, any policy section or prior statement the draft attributes to the employer, and the specific outcome requested — rather than a general 'proofread it,' matching the module's fabrication-in-formal-documents theme.

prompt: Sort each appointment-prep request by whether it's the safe, organizational use this lesson describes, or a diagnostic use to avoid.

categories.label: Safe — organizational
items: “Turn these symptom notes into a one-page summary organized by priority”
“Help me write three specific questions to ask about this medication side effect”

categories.label: Avoid — diagnostic
items: “Based on these symptoms, what condition do I most likely have?”
“Tell me how serious this new symptom is”

hints: Organizational requests reshape information you already have. Diagnostic requests ask it to generate new medical judgment about your body.
The second category is exactly what lesson 5 of this module names as the line not to cross.
explanation: Turning notes into a summary and drafting specific questions both reshape information the person already has into something more usable — genuinely safe, organizational uses. Asking what condition is likely, or how serious a symptom is, both ask the model to generate a medical judgment it has no way to properly ground — no exam, no full history, no ability to order tests — which is the diagnostic line this module's fifth lesson names directly.

prompt: You have a 20-minute specialist appointment next week and three months of scattered symptom notes. Write the actual prompt you'd use to get a usable summary, applying both this lesson's organizational boundary and its length/priority fix.
hints: Bound the request to organizing, not assessing, and name a specific length and priority structure.
Reference the actual constraint — the real appointment length — not a vague 'keep it short.'
explanation: A strong prompt does both things this lesson names: “Here are my symptom notes from the last three months [pasted in]. Organize them into a one-page summary for a 20-minute specialist appointment — list the top three things I most need addressed first, with everything else as brief background below. Don't assess what might be causing anything, just help me organize what I already know so I can communicate it clearly.” The explicit length cap and priority order fix the three-page problem; the explicit 'don't assess' instruction keeps the request on the safe, organizational side of the line.

prompt: True or false: once an AI tool has produced a clear, readable plain-language summary of a legal or insurance document, that summary is safe to act on directly for any deadline or dollar figure it mentions.

config.statement: A clear plain-language summary is safe to act on directly for any deadline or dollar figure it mentions.
config.rubric: A full answer states false and explains that readability and authority are different properties — a summary is a comprehension aid, and for anything with a real deadline or amount at stake, the exact original wording (not the paraphrase) is what should be acted on.

hints: Recall the 'about two months' versus 'sixty calendar days' example — were they the same number?
What's the difference between understanding a document and being safe to act on a paraphrase of it?
explanation: False. Clarity in a summary tells you it's easy to read, not that its specific figures are precise enough to act on. A plain-language summary is genuinely useful for understanding what a document is broadly saying, but for a real deadline, dollar amount, or required action, the actual binding wording — not the paraphrase — is what a real decision should be based on.

prompt: You've received a dense, multi-page letter from a government agency about a benefits review. Write the prompt you'd use to extract exactly what you need to do and by when, applying this lesson's structured-and-quoted approach.
hints: Ask for deadlines, required documents, and actions specifically — not a general summary.
Require an exact quote for each item, not a paraphrase.
explanation: A strong prompt asks for a structured, quote-anchored extraction: “List every deadline, every document I need to submit, and every action this letter requires me to take. For each one, quote the exact sentence from the letter it comes from, so I can check it myself.” This surfaces buried actionable items and keeps each one traceable to the real text, rather than trusting a general summary's restatement of a deadline or requirement.

prompt: You want an AI tool to explain what a specific medical billing code and charge amount typically mean. Which is the safest way to ask?

options.text: “Explain what billing code 99214 with a $340 charge typically covers” — with no account number, name, or address included
Paste the entire explanation-of-benefits statement, including account number and full name, for full context
Paste the statement but only remove your name, keeping the account number for reference
Take a photo of the whole document and upload it directly

hints: What does explaining a billing code actually require to be present in the request?
The account number and full statement image both carry identifying detail the task doesn't need.
explanation: Explaining what a billing code and charge typically cover doesn't require an account number, a name, or an address — the first option accomplishes the exact same task with none of that identifying detail present. Pasting the full statement, keeping the account number 'for reference,' or uploading a photo of the whole document all include identifying strings the task never actually needed.

prompt: You're helping an aging parent understand a dense letter from their pharmacy benefits plan, which includes their full name, member ID, and a list of their current prescriptions. Describe exactly what you'd redact before asking an AI tool for help, and what you'd keep.
hints: Apply the stricter standard from this lesson's second pod — it's not your data, so the usual convenience tradeoffs don't apply the same way.
Keep whatever the actual question needs — usually the substance, not the identifiers.
explanation: A strong answer redacts the parent's full name, member ID number, and any account-identifying details, while keeping the substantive content the actual question needs — for instance the specific prescription names and the coverage question being asked about them (if that's genuinely necessary to the question) or a description of the plan language that's confusing. The reasoning should explicitly note that this is someone else's information, so the redaction should be at least as careful as it would be for the person's own data, not left to a convenience-driven judgment call made on their behalf.

prompt: Which of these is a genuinely safe, useful request for an AI tool, per this lesson's line?

options.text: “I already have a diagnosis of migraine — give me general educational information about typical triggers, so I can compare against my own patterns”
“I have a headache that's lasted three days — what condition do I have?”
“Is this headache serious enough that I should go to urgent care?”
“Look at these test results and tell me if anything looks concerning”

hints: Which option asks for general educational information about a condition already diagnosed, rather than a new assessment?
The other three each ask the model to diagnose, triage, or interpret results — the exact line from this lesson.
explanation: Requesting general educational information about an already-diagnosed condition stays on the organizational and educational side of the line — it doesn't ask the model to assess anything new about the person. Asking what condition a new symptom represents, whether it's serious enough to seek care, or to interpret test results are all forms of the diagnostic or triage judgment this lesson names as requiring an actual clinician.

prompt: A friend describes a new symptom to you and says an AI chatbot told them “this is probably nothing to worry about.” They're relieved and planning to skip calling their doctor. What would you actually say to them, using this lesson's reasoning?
hints: Focus on what the chatbot's answer can and can't actually be based on.
The point isn't to alarm them — it's to name what a reassuring answer here actually is and isn't evidence of.
explanation: A strong answer explains, without dismissing their relief, that the chatbot's reassurance isn't based on anything it can't actually access — no exam, no history, no ability to rule anything out — so a careful-sounding “probably nothing” carries much less weight than it feels like it does. The useful reframe from this lesson: a good-sounding answer to a triage-shaped question is a reason to still make the call and get a real assessment, not a substitute for one — especially since the cost of a quick call is low and the cost of skipping a genuine problem based on an unfounded reassurance isn't.

prompt: You're too exhausted to write a landlord letter about a needed repair from scratch. What's the safest way to use AI here?

options.text: Provide the actual details (what's broken, when you reported it, any prior correspondence) and check every specific fact in the draft before sending
Ask it to write a generic repair-request letter with no specifics, since any letter is better than none
Don't use AI at all for anything this consequential
Send whatever draft it produces without checking, since it read fluently

hints: Which option matches this module's actual guidance — draft-and-verify, not draft-blind or avoid entirely?
explanation: Providing real specifics and checking every factual claim before sending is exactly this module's approach — getting the letter written despite low energy, without letting an invented date or detail go out unchecked. Avoiding AI entirely ignores the real accommodation value; sending an unchecked or fact-free draft repeats the exact fabrication risk this module warns about.

prompt: You have a follow-up appointment in two days and a phone full of scattered notes about a worsening symptom. Write the prompt you'd use to prepare, keeping it on the safe, organizational side of this module's diagnostic line.
hints: Ask for organization and a question list, not an assessment of what's happening.
Name a length or priority constraint so the output is actually usable in a short appointment.
explanation: A strong prompt asks for organization within a real constraint, e.g.: “Here are my notes on this symptom over the last two weeks. Organize them into a half-page summary for a short follow-up appointment, prioritizing what's changed most. Then help me write three specific questions to ask. Don't tell me what you think is causing it — just help me organize and prepare.” This keeps the request organizational, bounds its length, and explicitly rules out the diagnostic framing this module warns against.

prompt: True or false: once an AI tool has translated a dense legal notice into plain language, the exact original wording no longer matters for anything.

config.statement: Once a legal notice is translated into plain language, the exact original wording no longer matters.
config.rubric: A full answer states false and explains that a plain-language version is a comprehension aid, but the exact original wording is what should be relied on for anything with a real deadline, dollar figure, or required action attached.

hints: Recall the 'about two months' versus 'sixty calendar days' example.
explanation: False. A plain-language translation helps with understanding what a document is broadly saying, but it doesn't replace the exact original wording where a real deadline, amount, or required action is at stake — those specific details should be verified against the actual quoted text, not the paraphrase, exactly as this module's third lesson demonstrates.

prompt: Sort each detail by whether it's safe to leave in when pasting a personal document into an AI tool, or should be redacted first.

categories.label: Safe to leave in
items: The specific billing code and dollar amount in question
The general type of appointment or service (e.g. 'physical therapy referral')

categories.label: Redact first
items: Your full account or policy number
Your exact home address

hints: The substance a task needs (a code, an amount, a general description) is usually safe. Specific identifying strings usually aren't needed for the task at all.
explanation: The billing code, dollar amount, and general service type are exactly the substance most tasks (explaining a code, drafting an appeal) actually need. Account numbers and exact addresses are identifying strings that almost no explanatory or drafting task requires — they can be removed with no loss to what the AI tool actually needs to help.

prompt: Put these four steps of handling a real piece of admin paperwork in the order this module builds them.

items: Redact identifying details the task doesn't actually need before pasting anything in
Provide the actual document, not a description of it, when asking for a draft or summary
For any deadline or dollar figure that matters, get the exact quoted wording, not a paraphrase
Check every specific fact the draft states against your real records before acting on it

hints: This follows the module's build order: protect first, ground the request, get precision on what matters, then verify before acting.
explanation: Redacting unneeded identifying details (lesson 4) is the first, protective step regardless of what comes after. Providing the actual document (echoing the research module, applied here) grounds whatever comes next. Getting exact wording for anything consequential (lesson 3) prevents a costly paraphrase error. Checking every specific fact before acting (lesson 1) is the final safeguard before anything gets submitted or relied on for real.

prompt: You're helping a sibling understand a dense letter about their own child's school accommodation plan — none of it is your own information. What changes about how you'd redact before using an AI tool?

options.text: The standard gets stricter, not the same — it's not your data or your decision to risk, so redact at least as carefully as you would your own
Nothing changes, since you're just trying to help
You can be more relaxed about it, since you have permission from your sibling to help
You should avoid using AI at all in any situation involving another person's document

hints: Recall this module's distinction between your own risk tolerance and someone else's information.
explanation: Per this module's fourth lesson, another person's private information — here, both the sibling's and the child's — isn't a decision you have standing to make trade-offs about on your own, even with good intentions and permission to help with the task. The right response is a stricter, more careful redaction habit, not the same standard, a looser one, or avoiding AI assistance altogether.

prompt: Think of a real piece of admin or a real health-related question from your own life recently. Name which of this module's five lessons applies most directly, and whether your actual habit matched what this module recommends.
hints: Be honest about the mismatch if there was one — that's the useful part of the answer.
If nothing comes to mind, imagine the next piece of paperwork you're likely to face and reason through it in advance.
explanation: A strong answer names something real and specific — an appeal, an appointment, a dense letter, a document with someone else's information, or a health question — correctly identifies which lesson's guidance applies, and gives an honest self-assessment of whether the actual habit matched it. As with earlier modules' practice sets, the value is in the honest audit, not a claim of having done everything right already.
